articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino leaving USMNT for Manchester United just months after signing new deal
articles.summary: The Argentine coach will lead the Americans against Haiti before taking over a struggling Premier League giant, leaving U.S. Soccer searching for a replaceme...
articles.body:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. — Barely 100 days into his second term as U.S. coach, Mauricio Pochettino is leaving.

Barring a last-minute snag, his expected move to Manchester United will become official Friday, Yahoo Sports has learned.

An expected midday announcement in England — and early morning in the U.S. — will end a whirling week of speculation and multiparty negotiations that unfolded not so quietly while he continued overseeing U.S. preparations at the national training center near Atlanta.

Sources said Pochettino, 54, will complete his two-year tenure with the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti — Saturday in Miami and Tuesday in Cincinnati — before taking charge of a storied Premier League club off to its worst start in 40 years.

U.S. Soccer officials have not commented on the situation all week.

Pochettino is scheduled to address the media early Friday, a common practice the day before a game.

Pochettino will return to his coaching roots on the European club circuit, where he worked for Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, among others, before dipping his toes into international waters for the first time with the U.S.

Pochettino had spoken with United on three separate occasions over the years but never received the luminous job. He is expected to debut Nov. 22 at Liverpool.

His U.S. finale will mark the end of a 37-match spell featuring a World Cup campaign that galvanized the nation for several weeks over the summer before a humbling, Round-of-16 defeat to Belgium.

The breakup comes a little more than three months after he and the U.S. Soccer Federation renewed their partnership with the expectation he would guide the team for four years and reach new heights at the 2030 World Cup.

But rehiring a coach with strong ties to the European scene — aside from the jobs, he has kept homes in London and Barcelona and never lived in the U.S. — came with the risk of him departing early. Even during the yearlong run-up to this year's 2026 World Cup, Pochettino was reportedly on Tottenham and AC Milan's short list.

The USSF is expected to begin its search for a replacement immediately.

Potential candidates include Nashville SC's B.J. Callaghan, an assistant on Gregg Berhalter's 2022 World Cup squad and later the interim head coach; former Belgium and Portugal boss Roberto Martinez; U.S. under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, who was hired over the summer to prepare the 2028 Olympic team; and Pelegrino Matarazzo, a New Jersey native with extensive European credentials who is now in charge of Spain's Real Sociedad.

Pep Guardiola — the famed former coach of Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City — would be on any team's list, though he seems much more likely to land in another European job and would probably demand a salary that dwarfed Pochettino's U.S.-record $6 million.

The USSF is not in any rush. Aside from having an opening just months into a nascent World Cup cycle, the U.S. will not play again with the full squad until late March. The next major tournament is the CONCACAF Gold Cup next summer. World Cup qualifying will begin no earlier than next fall.

The pathway to Pochettino's departure began Monday with reports out of England that he had emerged as United's top choice to succeed Michael Carrick, who was on the hot seat after just 10 months at the helm.

In subsequent days, United engaged in talks with Pochettino's representatives and the USSF, which had included a $10 million release clause in the contract the sides signed after the World Cup.

Carrick was fired Thursday, clearing the way for United to complete terms with Pochettino and finalize the USSF's fee.

After signing his new USSF deal in August, Pochettino set out to shape the next four years by introducing a dozen young players for a sweep of four home friendlies in the September-October window — a sign he was very much in it for the long run.

However, hours after opening camp Monday ahead of the Nations League quarterfinals, his long-term plans with the U.S. turned to quickly completing the United move.

articles.title: USA soccer sends emotional letter to players about pulling out of U-17 World Cup in Qatar amid Iran war
articles.summary: U.S. Soccer's letter to U-17 players reveals the emotional toll behind the Qatar World Cup withdrawal, citing the Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar.
articles.body: U.S. Soccer expressed its "shared disappointment" in a letter to players explaining its withdrawal from the upcoming U-17 World Cup in Qatar amid safety concerns surrounding the Iran war. The letter, obtained by Fox News Digital, praised the players and coaches for their preparation while explaining why the federation was canceling both its pre-tournament camp and participation in the competition. "We are writing to inform you of the difficult decision to cancel our World Cup pre-camp and our planned participation in the World Cup. We are extremely proud of the preparation by our players and coaches to represent the US in the World Cup," the letter said. TEAM USA WITHDRAWS FROM FIFA U-17 WORLD CUP AMID STATE DEPARTMENT TRAVEL WARNING IN MIDDLE EAST "Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances including the US State Department’s Level 3 Travel Advisory for Qatar and related directives for Embassy staff and families, we are no longer able to participate in the tournament. The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority." The withdrawal became public Wednesday, eight days before the tournament’s scheduled Nov. 19 start. The letter also instructed players to hold off on publicly discussing the decision until FIFA announced it, while telling them their clubs would receive official notification. "We will communicate this officially to your clubs today as well. We ask that you refrain from sharing this information or commenting publicly until such time that it has been communicated publicly by FIFA," the letter said. "Again, please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The State Department’s Oct. 23 advisory urges Americans to reconsider travel to Qatar because of the risk of armed conflict. U.S. government employees must obtain special authorization to travel there. The advisory cites attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces against civilian airports and other infrastructure in neighboring Saudi Arabia, warning that the hostilities could spread rapidly beyond the immediate area. It also identifies risks to civilian aviation from regional political and military tensions. Americans who travel to Qatar are urged to prepare to shelter in place and have an emergency departure plan that does not depend on U.S. government assistance. Fox News Digital previously reported that an Iranian missile struck Qatar’s Al-Udeid Air Base in March. Qatari officials reported no injuries. Fox News Digital also reported that nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families were ordered out of Saudi Arabia on Oct. 23 over safety concerns. For the American players, the withdrawal ends a World Cup opportunity less than a week after head coach Alex Aldaz announced his 21-player roster Nov. 6. The Americans were scheduled to open against Montenegro on Nov. 21, face Chile on Nov. 24 and finish Group J play against Algeria on Nov. 27. The roster included Philadelphia Union forward Malik Jakupovic, who scored eight goals during qualifying, and players affiliated with European clubs including AC Milan, Ajax and PSV. The United States earned its place in February, winning its qualifying group in St. Vincent and the Grenadines. The Americans beat the hosts 8-0 and St. Kitts and Nevis 10-0 before clinching qualification with a 1-1 draw against the Dominican Republic. Nine members of that qualifying squad were included on the World Cup roster. This year’s competition is the second under the tournament’s expanded annual, 48-team format and the second of five consecutive editions awarded to Qatar. articles.title: Kamario Taylor drops ‘never a doubt’ truth bomb on Mississippi State return
articles.summary: Mississippi State football received a massive boost in re-adding quarterback Kamario Taylor for 2027. Taylor’s new collegiate contract prevents a College Fo...
articles.body:
Mississippi State football received a massive boost in re-adding quarterback Kamario Taylor for 2027 . Taylor's new collegiate contract prevents a College Football Transfer Portal entry. Now the dual-threat broke his silence on coming back to the Bulldogs.

Taylor addressed his decision to ESPN's Sportscenter on Thursday following agreeing to his $7.5 million deal.

"The decision was already made in all honesty. There was never a doubt in my mind, there was never even options for me to leave here," Taylor shared to Sportscenter.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Taylor's decision comes amid Mississippi State's five-game losing streak and him losing the rest of his 2026 campaign. Taylor left the Oklahoma game early and never returned . So his 2027 return hands Bulldog fans something to cheer for during this slide.

Furthermore, Taylor's return likely will attract more wide receivers and other skill position recruits. Now coach Jeff Lebby and his staff can paint the picture of how future Bulldogs can work with the dynamic passer and runner.

Taylor elevated the Bulldogs to a 4-0 start that included beating South Carolina 41-34, which was unranked at the time. Now that same Gamecocks team rose to No. 17 overall in the College Football Playoff poll released on Tuesday. Which makes the Bulldogs' win over them a high quality one.

Despite the 4-5 mark, Mississippi State can still clinch a bowl spot with two more victories. It starts with facing Auburn at Starksville on Saturday, with the Tigers coming in at 5-4 overall under first-year coach Alex Golesh. Tennessee Tech follows next in a non-conference showdown for the Bulldogs. All before ending the season against Ole Miss, which owns three regular season losses.

articles.title: Megan Rapinoe, Julie Ertz and Jozy Altidore voted into the National Soccer Hall of Fame
articles.summary: national team standouts Megan Rapinoe, Jozy Altidore and Julie Ertz were among those elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on Thursday. David Beckham,...
articles.body:
Former U.S. national team standouts Megan Rapinoe, Jozy Altidore and Julie Ertz were among those elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on Thursday.

David Beckham, who helped grow soccer in the United States when he joined the LA Galaxy in 2007 and later as an owner of Inter Miami, was also voted into the Hall of Fame on the veteran ballot.

The group announced Thursday will be inducted on April 16 at the National Soccer Hall of Fame in Plano, Texas.

Rapinoe won a pair of Women's World Cup championships, an Olympic gold medal and the 2019 Ballon d'Or during her career. She was also honored with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, in 2022.

She retired from the national team in 2023 with 63 goals and 73 assists in 203 appearances. She also played for the Seattle Reign in the National Women's Soccer League from the league's first year in 2013 until her retirement.

Rapinoe was elected on the Hall of Fame's player ballot in her first year of eligibility. Her family, friends, and a group of fans surprised her with announcement of her election upon her arrival off a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

"To be alongside all the greatest players that have played for us, and played for our country alongside a bunch of my teammates and friends, recognized like that in this way just means you were successful and a part of great teams. So, I definitely was a part of some some great teams, and yeah, it's very special," Rapinoe said in a video posted to social media .

Altidore played in the World Cup twice and scored 42 international goals, to rank third in U.S. history, in 115 appearances for the national team. He also scored the winning goal for Toronto FC in the 2017 MLS Cup championship.

Ertz was considered among the best defensive midfielders in the world before her retirement in 2023 . She played in three Women's World Cups and was named U.S. Soccer's Player of the Year twice. She also played professionally for the NWSL's Chicago Red Stars from 2014 to 2021, before a short stint with Angel City in 2023.

Known for winning six Premier League titles while with Manchester United, Beckham looms large in the game's growth in the United States. He won back-to-back titles with the Galaxy, scoring 18 goals in 98 appearances. He exercised his option to buy an MLS expansion team in 2014, and Inter Miami joined the league in 2020.

Tatu, a Brazillian forward who scored 857 regular-season goals over a 21-year indoor soccer career, was also elected to the Hall of Fame on the veteran ballot. He is just the third indoor player to receive the honor.

Former U.S. national team coach Lothar Osiander was elected to the Hall of Fame on the builder ballot. Osiander coached the senior national team from 1986-88 and the under-23 team from 1988-92. He also had stints as head coach of the then-San Jose Clash and the LA Galaxy.

articles.title: Sydney Swans players will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
articles.summary: Four players had been under investigation after an alleged sexual assault after a game in Melbourne.
articles.body:
Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.

After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.

Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.

The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.

Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are reportedly looking into civil action.

"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.

A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.

Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.

Kamario Taylor said his decision to return to Mississippi State for the 2027 season, on an NIL deal that could be worth up to $9 million, was a no-brainer during an appearance on SportsCenter Thursday.

articles.title: La mejor de las últimas ligas
articles.standfirst: En esta campaña se están marcando 2,89 goles por partido siendo el mejor promedio desde la edición 2016-17
articles.summary: En esta campaña se están marcando 2,89 goles por partido siendo el mejor promedio desde la edición 2016-17
articles.body: Siguiendo la estela del Barcelona, que lleva camino de firmar un registro histórico con los 48 que lleva anotados y que le daría una proyección de 152 al final de la temporada, LaLiga esta promediando su mejor temporada realizadora de las últimas campañas. En los 119 partidos que se llevan disputados se han marcado goles lo que significa un promedio realizador de 2,89 tantos por encuentro. Esta cifra es la más alta de las últimas temporadas. Para encontrar un registro igual o mayor hay que remontarse a la edición liguera de 2016-17. En aquella campaña se anotaron en los 380 partidos disputados un número de 1.118 goles lo que dio un promedio de 2,94 tantos por encuentro. Desde entonces, no se han marcado tantos goles en a liga española como en la presente campaña. En la temporada pasada, la 2025-26, se lograron 1.024 tantos, con una media de 2,69 por partido, y no fue una mala campaña porque se rebasó la barrera del millar, algo que solo se había realizado una vez en las anteriores siete ligas. Y si la 2016-17 es la más realizadora de los últimos años, la actual edición de LaLiga es la tercera pues en segunda posición de este podio está lo realizado en la 2012-13 cuando se marcaron 1.101 goles (con una media de 2,90 por partido). Si se mantiene este ritmo anotador, la cifra proyectada de goles al término de esta campaña 2026-27 sería de 1.098 goles, muy cerca de los 1.101 de la 2012-13 y a una distancia razonable de los 1.118 de la 2016-17. La liga con un mejor registro con 38 jornadas disputadas. El récord lo tiene la liga 1996-97 con 1.271 goles, pero con 42 jornadas disputadas. El principal motivo de las buenas cifras goleadoras de LaLiga en esta temporada es el acierto de los veinte equipos integrantes de la competición cuando actúan como visitantes. De los 344 goles marcados en esta temporada, 152 los han anotado los equipos que han actuado como foráneos. En cada partido de esta liga, los equipos visitantes tienen una media de 1,52 goles que es la misma cifra que se logró en la 2016-17, en la que marcaron 486 dianas, la más alta de los últimos años. Por contra, lo equipos que han actuado como locales tienen una media de 1,61 goles por partido (192 tantos) que es el octavo mejor registro de las últimas temporadas. Por tanto, si la 2026-27 quiere asaltar el récord de goles en 38 jornadas, los equipos cuando juegan en su campo deberían mejorar de cara a la portería contraria. Pero aunque los números de goles en esta temporada de la liga han mejorado, aún está por debajo de otras ligas. La Bundesliga es la más realizadora (3,48 goles por partido), seguida por la Serie A (3,11) y La Ligue 1 (2,96), siendo la Premier (2,73) es la peor de las cinco grande

articles.title: Álex Valle: “Dentro de la locura de Cesc por el fútbol, jugamos para divertirnos”
articles.standfirst: El lateral del Como, concentrado con la sub-21, desgrana en MARCA su adiós al Barça, el aprendizaje escocés y el reto de una Champions en Italia viven como un regalo
articles.summary: El lateral del Como, concentrado con la sub-21, desgrana en MARCA su adiós al Barça, el aprendizaje escocés y el reto de una Champions en Italia viven como un regalo
articles.body: Álex Valle (Badalona, 2004) se ha hecho un nombre en la penumbra. Canterano del Barça, ha tejido su carrera lejos de los focos: Andorra, Levante, Celtic de Glasgow y un estimulante Como con el que se ha subido al tren de la Champions como equipo revelación. Hoy es el lateral izquierdo de referencia de la sub-21 de David Gordo, que hoy abre en Almendralejo ante Japón (19.00 horas, Teledeporte) una ventana que mira ya al Europeo de 2027. En ese alto en el camino, en la concentración de Las Rozas, Álex Valle atiende a MARCA para hablar de sus aventuras y de un presente difícilmente mejorable. P. Es la primera vez que viene solo un jugador del Como en una convocatoria de la sub-21. R. Yo creo que sí, porque entre Jesús, Jacobo… Bueno, hubo una que se fueron los dos lesionados y me dejaron aquí solo. Jacobo esta vez me ha dejado tirado, pero es por una buena oportunidad, así que se lo voy a permitir. Lleva un inicio de temporada bueno el tío, metiendo goles, que era lo que le faltaba el año pasado. P. David Gordo, seleccionador sub-21, dijo que de usted nunca se habla. ¿Por qué cree que no se habla de Álex Valle? R. Gracias al míster, lo primero. Me lo comentó mi padre. Yo hago mi trabajo y creo que lo estoy haciendo bien este año, y eso se refleja en que estoy viniendo convocado. Que se hable más o que se hable menos… Estoy en un equipo en el que no solo lo hago bien yo, también hay un tal Nico Paz, un tal Jacobo y muchísima más gente. No tengo ningún problema. ¿Me voy a quejar por estar aquí convocado? P. En el lateral izquierdo de la absoluta están Cucurella y Grimaldo. ¿Se fija mucho en ellos? R. Son buenísimos, son buenos profesores. Y si no son ellos, también hay otros laterales izquierdos en España que son muy buenos. España está asegurada en todas las posiciones. Yo estoy muy contento de estar aquí, se hable o no se hable de mí. P. ¿Es más de estar fuera del foco o agradece el protagonismo? R. Nunca he sido de estar en el foco ni me gusta. Me considero un jugador de equipo, pero por encima del equipo en el que estoy. Creo que la posición del lateral está un poco infravalorada, porque hay veces que es incluso una putada: hay que hacer un poco de todo. P. ¿Eso se lo transmite Cesc? R. El míster siempre lo dice, que el lateral tiene que entender de todo un poco y leer bien el juego para saber en cada partido lo que tiene que hacer: si es más de ataque, más de defensa… Hay que ser inteligente. Cuando la gente que sabe, como el entrenador, conoce el valor que tiene, no importa tanto que no se hable del lateral en los medios. P. ¿Se siente más defensa o centrocampista? R. Es difícil, porque cada partido es distinto. Si juego con un extremo más interior, me siento más carrilero; si hay alguien que tiene que estar más abierto, me da la libertad de meterme por dentro cuando leo que lo tengo que hacer. Y no solo a mí: también a los extremos, al delantero, a Nico en la media punta. Si entiendes el juego y lo que está pasando, te puedes permitir esa libertad de moverte. P. Las comparaciones son odiosas, pero ¿con qué se compararía? R. Ahora mismo no te sabría decir. Antes mi referente era Jordi Alba, y podría decir que ahora también. Me encantaba porque es súper inteligente, y tuve la suerte de coincidir con él en unos entrenos al final de temporada con Xavi y verlo en persona. Ves cómo entiende el fútbol… Sí, es mi referente. P. David Gordo también dijo que no le había tocado pasar por situaciones fáciles. ¿A qué se refería? R. Supongo que a mi historial de equipos. No es fácil que cada seis meses o cada año tengas que salir, ir a un Andorra, a Segunda con 17 años, con un entrenador especial como Eder Sarabia. Luego un contexto totalmente distinto, viviendo solo con mi novia en Valencia, otro fútbol. Y después Glasgow, todo cambiado, con una forma de jugar un poco de medio centro; ahí me costó más, empecé un poco jodido. Así que no lo he tenido fácil, estoy con el míster en eso. Ahora he encontrado un poco la estabilidad. P. Aun con lo difícil, ¿lo cambiaría por algo? R. No lo cambiaría por nada. Pude tener la oportunidad de quedarme en el Barça, pero a día de hoy no me arrepiento de nada, porque han sido tantas cosas diferentes, tantos estímulos, tantas maneras de vivir… Con mi novia, mis dos perros, viviendo en Italia, disfrutando de la vida y del fútbol. Soy un afortunado. He tenido momentos difíciles, pero se agradecen. P. Siendo tan joven, ¿por qué no decidió quedarse en Barcelona? R. No estaba claro que me quedara sí o sí en el primer equipo; igual estaba en el Barça B, no lo sabía. En aquella pretemporada me encontré muy bien con Flick, me encanta como entrenador y me gustaba mucho su idea. Estuve jugando de lateral derecho y me sentí muy cómodo; vi que era una posición abierta para el futuro. Pero en ese momento me sentía lateral izquierdo y ahí no había espacio: estaban Gerard y Baldé. Tuve una charla muy amistosa y honesta con Flick, y yo tenía el Celtic, la oportunidad de jugar Champions y salir otra vez. Me tiré de cabeza. P. Ahora el Barça tiene esa posición cogida con pinzas. A lo mejor Flick habría pensado que usted le vendría bien… R. Como en la vida y en el fútbol, no se puede saber nada. Con la vuelta de Cancelo, Balde, que me parece un lateral increíble, y Gerard de central, que lo está haciendo muy bien… El fútbol, quién me lo iba a decir. Y quién me iba a decir que igual no estaría ahí si me hubiera quedado ese año. Prefiero no pensar en eso. Soy un afortunado. P. Su padre, siendo perico, quizá respiró aliviado al no tener que seguir apoyando al Barça. R. No te creas. Mi padre ahora vive mucho el fútbol de su hijo; allá donde voy se pone nervioso, lo vive muchísimo. Antes era más intenso conmigo, ahora me da mi espacio y elige bien los momentos. Se lo agradezco, porque hay días que no apetece, pero otros sí me gusta hablar de fútbol, y a él le gusta bastante. P. ¿Hay charla después de los partidos? R. Hay algún textito que habría que revisar, pero no le puedo decir nada. P. Se acabó yendo al Celtic, equipo histórico, pero fuera de la órbita del fútbol de primer nivel. ¿Le surgieron dudas? R. Totalmente, hay que ser realista. La vida en Barcelona está muy tranquila, estás en el club de tu vida y había una mínima oportunidad real de quedarte. Habría que preguntarle a mi yo de hace tres años qué le pasaba por la cabeza. Pero tomé la decisión firme, lo decidimos con mi familia, mi novia y mis representantes, y cuando cojo algo me lo tomo al pie de la letra. Trabajé mucho, porque el Celtic es una liga diferente, muy física, muy jodida; aunque no haya tanto nivel técnico, cuesta ganar. P. ¿Pensó que irse a una liga casi desconocida era un sacrificio? R. No lo pensé así, porque sabía que el escaparate de la Champions era un factor clave. Había visto al Celtic un par de partidos, había hablado con Brendan Rodgers y su manera de jugar me llamó la atención. Acabé aprendiendo conceptos de medio centro que aquí me vinieron de perlas: al principio no jugábamos tanto así, pero cuando el equipo fue evolucionando, saber un poco más de todo me fue genial. P. Y al año, llama el Como. R. Me surgió la oportunidad de volver porque no había jugado ni siquiera en una gran liga, y Cesc me dio mucha confianza con un par de llamadas. Fui para allá y lo demás es historia. P. Llega al Como y quedan décimos el primer año. ¿Imaginaba que crecería tan rápido? R. Así de rápido no lo imaginaba nadie. Llegamos en invierno, con once o doce fichajes, estábamos jodidos, peleando por no descender, y acabamos ganando ocho de diez partidos. Pero cuando hablas de fútbol con Cesc y te cuenta su idea, te das cuenta de que es muy ambicioso, que tiene mentalidad de querer ganar y no tenerle miedo a nada ni a nadie. Y eso va relacionado con ser español; me siento orgulloso, porque tenemos una gran mentalidad. Con esa mentalidad se han alcanzado objetivos antes de tiempo. P. ¿Qué tiene Cesc que no tienen otros entrenadores? R. Aparte de esa mentalidad que te transmite, las ganas de comerte el campo, sabe comunicar muy bien, es un fuerte suyo. Tiene grandes ideas, y no solo él, también todo su staff, que está muy preparado. Él es el encargado de transmitirlas con los vídeos, las charlas, en el campo… Mete mucha caña, es intensito. Alguna vez se mete a algún rondo y lo disfruta. P. ¿Sigue teniendo toque? R. Tiene toque, hay que tirársela al pie, pero tiene, sí. P. El histórico 1-9 al Lens en Champions. R. No nos lo esperábamos. La Champions es un regalo, un premio que nos hemos ganado, y lo estamos disfrutando. Quedan cuatro partidos que no están mal, estamos con nueve puntos e intentaremos sacar más y clasificar. No hay que bajar la cabeza. P. ¿En algún momento pensaron en bajar el pie del acelerador? R. No. Estaba también Martin Baturina, que se comió el 8-2 del Bayern al Dinamo de Zagreb hace unos años, y después del partido estaba súper contento porque ya tenía la historia positiva. Yo estaba un poco en shock cuando entraba el sexto, el séptimo… Pasaba todo muy rápido. Fue raro, pero estábamos muy contentos. Es algo histórico para nosotros, esa camiseta la voy a guardar siempre. Una sensación extraña. La primera acabó 0-3 y dijimos: “Van a entrar fuertes, estos se meten con un gol, el estadio empieza a calentarse”. Salimos fuertes y nos entraron los goles rapidísimo. P. ¿Se habla de Champions y Scudetto en el vestuario? R. A ver, nosotros no nos ponemos ningún objetivo, porque es nuestra primera Champions. Jugué dos o tres partidos con el Celtic, pero esta es prácticamente mi primera experiencia, y como yo hay muchos. No teníamos expectativas: vamos a disfrutar. La motivación viene sola, porque la Champions para mí es lo mejor que hay, el himno es una pasada. Ahora que estamos, a pelear con los mejores. P. Con tantas competiciones, ¿qué hace para desconectar? R. Tenemos poco tiempo, está siendo caótico, es mi primera vez con esto. Desde la última convocatoria no hemos parado, un par o tres de días libres. Para desconectar tengo la suerte de que mi novia está conmigo y mis dos perros me dan la vida, estoy casi todo el tiempo con ellos. Los chavales vivimos cerquita, hacemos alguna cosa, tenemos el ping-pong, vemos fútbol para variar… Poco más, no necesitamos mucho. P. ¿Cesc les pide que no desconecten del todo? R. Nos mantiene un poco, dice que no nos desconectemos mucho de esto. Hay que tener tu tiempo para despejar la mente, pero siendo conscientes de que es una época concurrida: al principio se define mucha parte de la temporada, si te mantienes arriba o empiezas a aflojar. Hay que estar metido. P. La piña española en Como. R. Es algo muy positivo de estar aquí, hay muchos jóvenes, bastantes con novia, y ellas son muy amigas, están superfelices. Por ese lado estamos tranquilos. P. Para terminar, lo que más le ha sorprendido de Cesc. R. Su cercanía. Lo dice todo el mundo: es muy honesto, se puede hablar muy fácil con él. La relación con el entrenador es muy buena, es buena gente. Es metódico, pero dentro de esa locura por el fútbol que tiene; al final jugamos para divertirnos.

articles.title: La luz al final del túnel
articles.standfirst: Rodrygo y Asencio siguen quemando etapas, aunque el club no maneja una fecha cerrada y priorizará evitar riesgos
articles.summary: Rodrygo y Asencio siguen quemando etapas, aunque el club no maneja una fecha cerrada y priorizará evitar riesgos
articles.body: El Real Madrid empieza a ver la luz al final del túnel con Raúl Asencio y Rodrygo Goes. Los dos futbolistas continúan avanzando en sus respectivos procesos de recuperación tras volver a pisar el césped y realizar ejercicios con balón. Una imagen positiva que confirma su progresión y alimenta el optimismo en Valdebebas, aunque todavía queda camino por recorrer antes de que puedan reincorporarse al trabajo con el grupo. En el club no quieren precipitar acontecimientos ni establecer una fecha de regreso que pueda condicionar su evolución. Hay distintas ventanas sobre la mesa, pero la prioridad será que ambos vuelvan en plenitud de condiciones y sin asumir riesgos innecesarios. Rodrygo afronta la recuperación más larga de los dos. El brasileño cayó lesionado el pasado 2 de marzo, durante el encuentro de Liga frente al Getafe, y las pruebas confirmaron una rotura del ligamento cruzado anterior y del menisco externo de la rodilla derecha. Fue intervenido quirúrgicamente el 10 de marzo y desde entonces ha ido superando diferentes fases de rehabilitación. Ya en septiembre comenzó a trabajar sobre el césped y a finales de ese mes incorporó el balón a sus ejercicios. Ahora, más de ocho meses después de la lesión, sigue progresando, aunque las previsiones más prudentes sitúan su regreso entre finales de diciembre y enero de 2027. El caso de Asencio es diferente, pero también ha requerido paciencia. El canterano arrastraba desde hacía meses una fractura por estrés en la tibia derecha que no terminó de resolverse con tratamiento conservador. Finalmente, el 1 de octubre pasó por el quirófano para solucionar definitivamente el problema y comenzar una nueva rehabilitación. La previsión inicial apuntaba a un periodo de entre dos y cuatro meses, pero el propio futbolista reconoció recientemente que su evolución está siendo mejor de lo esperado y que incluso podría acortar los plazos. Sin embargo, tampoco quiere ponerse una fecha: su intención es completar correctamente todas las etapas antes de volver a competir. Desde el entorno del jugador son optimistas con su regreso a mediados de diciembre... con el objetivo de realizar entrenamientos parciales con el grupo de cara a una recuperación exprés: “Vamos a acortar los plazos”, aseguró a El Chiringuito el 2 blanco. Con ambos trabajando ya sobre el césped, la enfermería del Real Madrid queda reducida a sus dos nombres, una noticia especialmente positiva para Mourinho después de un inicio de temporada condicionado por los problemas físicos que se arrastraban del año pasado. El horizonte empieza a despejarse y el cuerpo técnico espera recuperar progresivamente a los dos futbolistas, pero no habrá prisas.

articles.title: Virgil van Dijk: What happens next for Liverpool captain?
articles.summary: Virgil van Dijk says he is in no panic about his contract situation at Liverpool - BBC Sport takes a look at what could happen with his future.
articles.body:
After Liverpool beat Brighton in October, Virgil van Dijk went upstairs to the Boardroom at Anfield and met up with Alan Hansen.

It was Van Dijk who, at the end of the 2024-25 season, asked the former Liverpool and Scotland defender to present him with the Premier League trophy and this time they posed for a picture that inevitably did the rounds on social media.

Whenever the time comes for Van Dijk to move on from Liverpool , he will go down as arguably their greatest centre-half, alongside Hansen. The question now is whether he will finish his career at Anfield like Hansen did in 1991.

Van Dijk's contract expires next summer and, even if the 35-year-old insisted this week that he was in no panic, it is a topic that will be a source of debate until a decision is made.

"Let's see what the season brings. I've had an amazing time already so far. If that will be extended, that's the case. If not, then I will go somewhere else," the Liverpool captain told reporters at Selhurst Park.

Two seasons ago, with Van Dijk in a similar situation, there was a similar sense of calm and come April 2025 he signed a two-year-deal.

Judging by Van Dijk's comments there is a feeling of him wanting to stay, but both he and Liverpool have an important decision to make.

Aside from a poor error against Villarreal in the Champions League, Van Dijk has shown this season that his standards haven't dropped.

His partnership with Jeremy Jacquet, who joined in the summer, is going from strength to strength and Van Dijk has played every minute in the Premier League since the start of last season.

A "little niggle" has affected him in recent weeks and this is the first international window he has missed with the Netherlands since Euro 2020, but it isn't a major cause for concern.

Liverpool have lost a number of senior figures in recent years but Van Dijk remains a leader in every form, and that was evidenced by his suggestion to Andoni Iraola that the squad should visit the museum at Anfield to learn more about the club's history.

At Crystal Palace on Sunday, it spoke volumes of Van Dijk's character that he came over to a group of reporters and asked if they wanted to speak to him, rather than the other way around. He regularly fronts up, regardless of the result.

Van Dijk is certainly not the force he was under Jurgen Klopp but he remains an elite centre-half and the stats justify that.

Per 90 minutes this season in the Premier League, he averages 60.7 successful passes per game, wins possession 3.5 times and makes 7.1 clearances. He has a 75% success in duels and 79% when it comes to aerial duels.

In his first full season at the club, in 2019-20, he averaged 72.4 successful passes per game, won possession 5.1 times and made 5.3 clearances. He had a 76% success in duels and 75% when it came to aerial duels.

That said, the Liverpool hierarchy will have seen the way the situation with Mohamed Salah unfolded last year and will be keen to avoid a repeat. After a stellar season in 2024-25, Salah's numbers plummeted in 2025-26.

Liverpool have a number of young centre-backs within their ranks, from Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni to the likes of Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye, but letting Van Dijk go would be a risk and leave a gaping hole.

He didn't take a pay cut in 2025 and continues to earn a salary understood to be in the region of £400,000 a week.

Joe Gomez, 29, is also out of contract this summer and Liverpool do have an option to buy Ronald Araujo, 27, at the end of the season from Barcelona but there would be a clear loss of experience and leadership if Van Dijk leaves.

For sporting director Julian Ward, the future of the Dutchman will be a priority over the coming months.

No resolution to contract talks expected soon

Providing he is fit, Van Dijk will make his 390th appearance for Liverpool when they take on Manchester United after the international break.

And given his consistency, he is likely to reach 400 appearances by the end of the year. He would become only the 28th Liverpool player to do so.

The 36 goals he has scored for Liverpool is the most for a defender at the club.

In terms of a resolution with his contract, this is likely to be one where both parties bide their time and, given that the existing relationships are strong and there's a mutual respect, it would not be a surprise to see negotiations go into 2027.

Come January, Van Dijk will be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club and as such, AC Milan and Juventus are monitoring the situation.

Sources in Turkey are also hopeful that they could tempt him to make the same move as Salah if an extension isn't agreed at Liverpool but, as it stands, it would be quite a surprise if Van Dijk moved on this summer.

articles.title: Erling Haaland: How Wales aim to stop Norway’s Man City star again
articles.summary: Erling Haaland can seem unstoppable - but Wales managed it a month ago. In Norway on Saturday, they hope the plan will work again.
articles.body:
It is a question many have asked but only a few have answered successfully. How do you stop Erling Haaland?

Wales will be faced with that daunting task when they travel to Oslo on Saturday to face Norway in the Nations League.

With a record 65 goals in just 59 games for his country – not to mention the hundreds he has scored for Manchester City and his previous clubs – Haaland has conquered most defences he has encountered.

But Wales managed to shackle him during their 2-1 win in Cardiff a month ago. In that sense, they have a blueprint to keep the fearsome striker at bay.

"You're talking about trying to deal with one of the best players in his position in the world, and we've been seeing that for several years now," says Wales head coach Craig Bellamy.

"He's different to what you would normally have to deal with. He has the profile of everything you want in a player, and that's quite rare.

"It's a collective responsibility, not just an individual one."

Bellamy felt his team needed to take a calculated risk.

Some opponents have tried to sit back and defend deep against Haaland, but that can give him more time and space, more ways to wreak havoc.

Others have opted for a more confrontational, physical approach – not always wise against this powerful, 6ft 5in specimen.

Then there is the option of pressing high up the field. That can leave you exposed to balls over the top, which Haaland can race on to by using his raw pace.

Crucially, however, it can deny him – and, importantly, his talented team-mates – that time and space to inflict damage.

High-risk but high-reward, that is the route Bellamy chose.

"Drive up and don't let him dictate," he explains. "It's easier said than done because then you could turn around and say to me, 'Why are you playing a high line against Haaland?' Trust me you don't want to, but you can't have him dictating the game.

"That's true of all players, really, but it's much harder when someone is getting in your face and stopping you from having time on the ball.

"A good player can look like a top player if you give him time. A top player can look world-class if you give him time. A world-class player might then have a chance of looking like an ordinary or good player, if you don't allow him time.

"Putting pressure on the ball is always important for us, and I thought we did that really well that night."

Keep the ball, stop Odegaard and cut off the supply

Haaland was limited to 24 touches at Cardiff City Stadium. Anyone who has watched him play will know that is not unusual for the 26-year-old, who can drift in and out of a game around the pitch, only to come alive at key moments in the penalty area.

The more significant statistic is that he only had two shots, with only one on target, a header straight at Wales goalkeeper Danny Ward.

Prevention is better than a cure, and what Wales did effectively on that occasion was to cut off the supply of chances for Norway's talismanic frontman.

That was no mean feat considering that the Scandinavians' creator in chief is captain Martin Odegaard, one of the Premier League's most inventive playmakers and the man who led Arsenal to the title last season.

So as well as the defenders tasked with handling Haaland and his fellow forwards Fulham's Oscar Bobb and Andreas Schjelderup of Benfica, midfielders such as Ethan Ampadu had crucial roles to play in negating the attacking influence of Odegaard and his midfield colleagues.

"You have to consider the distance between Ethan and Haaland," Bellamy adds. "You can't open up the middle too much because balls are going to come into his feet. You have to get your distances right, be side-on and make sure you're aware of his runs.

"He has the ability to take a team on, but he also has the willingness to make those runs.

"It's also important how we use the ball. If we use it well, develop our possession and move up the pitch, he has to work. He has to run and get back."

Since Bellamy took charge in the summer of 2024, Wales' average share of possession in matches has rocketed.

They have had to make do with less of the ball in this Nations League campaign against Norway, Portugal and Denmark – and Bellamy believes his side could improve in that regard.

He has said Wales will be going "all out" for victory in Oslo on Saturday and, if they can stay on the front foot and make Norway defend, that is certainly one way of keeping Haaland out of the game.

"You have to be on it against these teams because they have many individual players who can create something out of nothing," says Dan James, who scored Wales' first goal in the 2-1 win.

"Our distances [between players] were really good. Odegaard is a unique player. He'll get the ball anywhere so it's hard as a defence. They want you to jump out and I think they showed that with their goal with the ball for Oscar Bobb and he's finished it well.

"We showed our resilience and it was about limiting their chances and I thought we did that.

"Odegaard played some great balls in behind but, to the very last minute, we defended really well, not just the defenders but the whole unit, from the forwards back.

"I thought we defended really well on the day, and we've got to be great again on Saturday."

Wales will be forced into at least one change in Oslo, with Swansea City centre-back Ben Cabango – who got Haaland's shirt after the game in Cardiff – missing through suspension.

The good news for Wales is that first-choice centre-back Joe Rodon, who was injured for the previous game, is available after returning for Leeds United last weekend.

"Ben Cabango and Ben Davies have both done really well against him [Haaland], but the work has to be done in front of them. If it isn't, you expose the defenders," Bellamy says.

"Against this type of player, it doesn't matter how good an individual defender is. We've seen over the last four or five years how difficult it becomes for one player to cope with what Haaland brings."

Taking on Haaland alone is not advisable. If you face the challenge together, however, as Wales showed just a month ago, you can stop the seemingly unstoppable.

articles.title: Tony Pulis column: From sending postcards to receiving texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack
articles.summary: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains some of the different ways a manager can leave a club, whether they have been sacked or resigned.
articles.body:
When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

'Every manager needs to think about their cardboard box'

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth , and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

articles.title: Northern Ireland v Ukraine: Who makes your starting team?
articles.summary: Ahead of Northern Ireland's Nations League outing with Ukraine in Belfast, who would you pick in your starting team at Windsor Park?
articles.body:
After an impressive quadruple-header to kick off the Nations League, Northern Ireland are back in action and it's time for you to be the boss.

Michael O'Neill's young side did not concede a goal as away victories over Georgia and Ukraine were joined by two goalless draws at home to Hungary and the Georgians, which leave Northern Ireland top of League B2 after four matches.

Now, they will look to finish the job and earn promotion to League A as Ukraine visit Belfast on Saturday, before a trip to Hungary on Tuesday to close out the group.

But who would you pick if you were in charge of Northern Ireland? Weigh up some of the key selection dilemmas before having your say.

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

Of the 54 teams in the Nations League, Northern Ireland are the only side yet to concede a goal after four rounds of matches.

It's all the more impressive when you consider O'Neill is without two Premier League level defenders, in the form of Liverpool's Conor Bradley, a long-term absentee, and Daniel Ballard, who was injured in the first match of the campaign in Georgia in September.

O'Neill has a plethora of options, both at the heart of defence and out wide.

At centre-back, youngsters Tom Atcheson and Ruairi McConville impressed in the quadruple-header, while O'Neill could also utilise the experience of Paddy McNair or Ciaron Brown.

There are also several options at right-back, with Trai Hume, the in-form Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer - who can also play at left-back along with Justin Devenny - all available.

In goal, first-choice Pierce Charles has fresh competition in the shape of Manchester United stopper Dermot Mee.

Who would you pick to keep the run of clean sheets going?

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Trai Hume has become something of a Swiss army knife option for both Northern Ireland and at Sunderland with his versatility.

Usually a right-back, Hume has often been utilised further forward on the right wing by Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris this season.

For Northern Ireland, the 24-year-old has played right across the defensive line when called upon.

With Conor Bradley fit and on the right flank, Hume would often feature as the right of three centre-backs, but he has also been deployed in both full-back positions.

Then, in October, he started in the centre of midfield against Ukraine and did not look out of place with a composed performance in a 3-0 win.

His versatility can only be a positive for Northern Ireland, but where would you play him to get the best out of both player and team?

Finding the back of the net has long been an issue for Northern Ireland, and despite the huge promise of this young team, they do still lack an out-and-out goalscorer.

Jamie Donley has been tasked with leading the line in recent matches, and he has been in good form at club level for Luton Town, albeit in a different role to the one his fills at international level.

His Luton team-mate Callum Marshall is another attacking option, and he can also be used out wide.

Josh Magennis is more of a target man option as he closes in on a century of Northern Ireland caps, while, at the other end of the experience scale, Braiden Graham is on the fringes of the first team with Everton and Eoin Kenny is untested having played just one Championship fixture since joining Portsmouth from Dundalk.

Who would you pick to lead the line against Ukraine on Saturday?

articles.title: Chelsea vs Man City: Mary Fowler reveals her side's latest evolution as we ask: Are City more dangerous than ever?
articles.summary: Manchester City have a new trump card, and forward Mary Fowler explains why it should be celebrated ahead of facing serial WSL winners Chelsea on Saturday; follow dedicated coverage of Chelsea vs Man City in our live blog this weekend; kick-off 1.30pm
articles.body:
City did not need to revolutionise the way they worked to reach this point, only the way they thought. Before Jeglertz, title talk was taboo. Under him it's mandated to such an extent it's written on the walls of their training base.

Because how does one learn the habits of a champion if the subject is not part of the everyday playbook? The Swede never considered the Women's Super League title aspirational, even in year one. How can it be at a club like Manchester City? All the tools are there.

Except of course winning silverware is not always the reserve of the club's with the best resources and most versatile talent. Nor should it be. That is what keeps football exciting. And, crucially here, what drives City's group to want to reinvent ways football matches can be won no matter the circumstance.

Pretty football. Tick. Threat from open play and set-pieces. Check. Stacks of goals from all over the pitch. Mastered. What else?

Perhaps the only critique of this near-perfect side is how they perform when they meet proper resistance. That is to say, when an opponent is so unyielding it renders their style of football, Jeglertz's preferred method, ineffective. Do City have a robust Plan B? And if they do, does it work against the best?

Off the back of scrapping to an important victory over London City Lionesses by less conventional means, Mary Fowler, who assisted the winner, explains City's new edge. "The way we won it, it was not our best performance in any way. But we won using a different style.

"All the girls knew the shift they would have to put in. There were loads of chances created against us but we put bodies on the line. We saved opportunities. Sometimes those kinds of wins feel deflating but we should actually celebrate it more.

"It was such a big shift for us to have to hold onto a win. It's a great mentality to keep belief until the bitter end. This group should be proud of that."

Man City's 2-1 victory in Bromley a fortnight ago was the first real examination of this new contingency plan in action. There were pinch-points towards the backend of last season where cracks appeared - losing to Brighton and getting lucky to sneak past Liverpool - but City remained in control of the title race.

Because actually it's often the year after winning a championship that is famously hardest.

City are having to find ways to adapt. Lauren Hemp called it 'winning ugly' last weekend, which is not a concept synonymous with the club or its manager. But is one that holds great reward if can be relied upon in small doses. Detaching gold standard performances from positive outcomes is something only elite sides can do.

"It's not our intention to win games that way," Fowler continues. "It always feels nicer when we have won in a way that feels comfortable. But being able to win ugly shows another side to this team. We aren't going to give up, we won't stop fighting for momentum and that one moment that can decide a game.

"That is something we showed in parts last season, we scored a lot of goals late in games. Whether it's an addition, or it's something we haven't had to use that often, I think it's a great quality to have and to recognise. It's good for confidence."

Chelsea, City's next opponents, used to be masters of this underrated art. Under Emma Hayes, the Blues were run like robots. In a good way. It made them domestically untouchable, such was their conviction to win by any means. Almost at any cost.

City have begun to lean into their example. "We love playing beautiful football but sometimes you have to scrap. Just because we have a plan to play a nice style doesn't mean it will always work. We have to have a fallback quality, even if it's messy. It's about getting stuff done."

But this not a copycat move. It's simply a pragmatic one, which safeguards against times where playing progressive football is less possible. In a meeting of the only two remaining unbeaten sides this weekend, an alternative strategy might come in particularly handy. "We're in a great place but we're fuelled to want to perform even better," says Fowler.

City have won just one of their last nine trips to Chelsea. Six of those were losses. And they arrive to a side that boast the best shot-per-90 rate of any team in WSL history. "It's a big game and a great match-up. Some wins have lacked performance so far but we have all the tools we need."

Jeglertz's side have already been made to endure this season. Their comeback victory over Arsenal in October was another example of the gritty nature by which results have been impressively ground out. City have already conceded double the amount of goals Chelsea have this term, and yet, are two point clear at the top of the table.

To be comfortable in the uncomfortable is definitely something new. Perhaps that makes the reigning champions more uncompromising than ever.

articles.title: Do Chelsea go into this weekend's top-of-the-table WSL clash with Manchester City as underdogs?
articles.summary: As the Women's Super League's top two sides prepare to do battle this weekend, should Chelsea be considered underdogs, or are they actually a dark horse? follow dedicated coverage of Chelsea vs Man City in Sky Sports' live blog this weekend; kick-off 1.30pm
articles.body:
But reality bites hard. The Blues lost their title to league and cup double winners Manchester City last term, in a season where they also suffered their second heaviest WSL defeat ever to the eventual champions.

That statement 5-1 drubbing back in February was the most obvious illustration of the gap that had appeared between superpowers. City were everything Chelsea used to be; a team relentlessly driven by title-winning standards. Every decision deliberately constructed to give them control and assert dominance.

If that was then, what is the state of play now?

This is the first WSL season to feature two unbeaten teams after nine matchdays since 2020-21. The table reads that Manchester City have the edge, but a deeper dive into the data presents a more nuanced case.

Stylistically, Sonia Bompastor's side have levelled up this year, shifting her setup from a more direct approach towards structured positional dominance. That is something she always wanted but did not necessarily have the personnel to perfect.

To play a more territorially dominant style, pressing in a player-oriented shape, Bompastor needed legs as well as a centre-forward who could lead the press with energy. Signing Katie McCabe from Arsenal and Melvine Malard from Manchester United have made it possible. The structure on the right has far more tactical coherence.

McCabe has slotted into a back three system whereby the wing-backs operate more like inverted forwards. The effectiveness of Sandy Baltimore and Ellie Carpenter out wide have been game-changing, and Malard as the focal point has helped, too, joining forces to create an attacking unit so versatile it's impossible to predict.

Chelsea lead every metric used to measure offensive performance, with a greater spread of goals than any other side. That fact serves a huge purpose. In a direct battle with Man City, Chelsea have more variance when mapping a route to goal and are creating a higher volume of quality chances. They are also the league's top scorers.

No player illustrates the maturation in style better than Kiera Walsh. Known most auspiciously for her reliability from deep, the England international has been given greater license to roam forwards this season, to great effect. She is now one of the key drivers of positional overloads, taking over 35 per cent of her touches in the final third.

With over half of the season still remaining, the midfielder is one off her best goal involvements return (currently 2G, 4A) and is creating chances with more regularity than ever before.

In fact, Bompastor has engineered a means by which her side can score from almost anywhere. Right the way through the spine of this team, there are playmakers. Each emboldened with a greater desire and commitment in forward areas. Lucy Bronze has been involved in four goals in eight WSL appearances from centre-back. Carpenter has scored four times herself.

But of course such risk has to be managed against a side like Man City. Their threat can be just as potent, if not as widespread. Bunny Shaw is personally responsible for 45 per cent of their respective goal tally, which totals one shy of Chelsea's.

In this battle of major powers, it's likely to be the more assured attack that wins out. Collectively, Chelsea have the statistical advantage. But if there is one individual capable of debunking such theory, it's undoubtedly Shaw.

articles.title: Bournemouth and Nottingham Forest battle Newcastle for highly-rated Santos starlet eyed by Bayern Munich
articles.summary: Bournemouth and Nottingham Forest are leading the Premier League chase to sign highly-rated Santos midfielder Gabriel Bontempo during the January transfer wi...
articles.body:
Bournemouth and Nottingham Forest are leading the Premier League chase to sign highly-rated Santos midfielder Gabriel Bontempo during the January transfer window. The English duo face stiff competition from Newcastle United for the 21-year-old Brazilian, who also attracted an enquiry from Bayern Munich over the summer.

According to TEAMtalk , the race for Bontempo is gathering pace as top-flight recruitment teams prepare mid-season approaches for one of South America's most sought-after emerging talents. Capable of operating effectively across several midfield and attacking roles, the versatile playmaker has developed rapidly at domestic level over recent months. His progress was recently rewarded with a senior international call-up to Carlo Ancelotti's latest Brazil squad .

The report states that Forest's acclaimed South American scouting network is strongly pushing the City Ground hierarchy to explore a formal move for the youngster ahead of the New Year. Recruitment chiefs in the East Midlands have already built a strong reputation for identifying talent in the region after their groundwork helped bring Murillo, Jair Cunha and Igor Jesus to the club's attention.

Meanwhile, the Cherries have emerged as serious contenders after lodging their own enquiries as they assess midfield options in case Alex Scott moves on. Having already demonstrated their willingness to recruit directly from the Brazilian market by signing Rayan last January, the south-coast outfit are keen to explore another deal in the country this winter.

European heavyweights join growing queue

Up on Tyneside, sporting director Ross Wilson and newly appointed head of recruitment Tomas Amaral are also monitoring the situation closely as they evaluate long-term additions. Both executives possess extensive knowledge of the South American market, while fellow English top-flight sides Brighton & Hove Albion and Brentford have also made initial enquiries as they track emerging prospects in Brazil.

Beyond the Premier League, insiders note that clubs across Italy, Spain and Germany are keeping tabs on his trajectory after the Bavarian giants asked about his situation during the summer window. That widespread continental interest underlines the fierce competition for his signature and ensures the Vila Belmiro hierarchy will face mounting pressure over the coming months.

Long contract strengthens negotiating stance

Despite the growing clamour from overseas suitors, Santos hold a commanding position ahead of the January market as Bontempo remains tied to the club until 2030. The Brazilian side have no intention of allowing one of their brightest stars to depart on the cheap and will demand a substantial financial package before considering any approach. Consequently, Forest, Bournemouth and their European rivals face tough negotiations to secure a winter transfer.

articles.title: How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd
articles.summary: With Mauricio Pochettino set to become Man Utd manager, we analyse if he can clear the tactical hurdles others haven't.
articles.body:
When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.

"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who is set to be the next manager of Manchester United.

In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.

Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.

"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.

"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."

Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.

For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.

In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.

But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.

Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.

Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.

This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.

At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.

With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.

But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.

Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.

This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.

Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.

In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.

If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.

These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.

This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.

Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.

This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.

The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.

By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.

Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.

Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.

This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.

And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.

"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.

Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.

For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.

Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.

The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.

There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.

Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.

Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.

With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.

But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.

Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.

His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.

Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".

Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.

"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.

United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.

If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.
